en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
The Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga,
Chapter on Saṅghādisesa Offenses.
3. The Training Rule on Going to Another Village Alone At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a nun who was a pupil of Bhaddā Kāpilānī, having quarreled with the nuns, went to a village where her kinsmen lived.
Not seeing that bhikkhunī, Bhaddā Kāpilānī asked the bhikkhunīs, “Where is so-and-so? She is not to be seen.
“Venerable lady, she has quarreled with the bhikkhunīs and is nowhere to be seen.
“Ladies, her family lives in such-and-such a village. Go there and search for her.”
The bhikkhunīs went there, saw that bhikkhunī, and said this to her: “Why have you come alone, noble lady?
Are you not molested? “I am not molested, noble ladies.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... [and so on]... were indignant, disparaged [her], and complained, saying:
“How indeed can a bhikkhunī travel alone from one village to another?
… [after questioning] … “Is it true, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhunī travels alone from one village to another?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How indeed, monks, can a bhikkhunī travel alone between villages?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiring of the faithless nor for the increase of the faithful…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, the bhikkhunīs should recite this training rule thus:
“Whichever bhikkhunī should travel alone to another village, that bhikkhunī too has committed an offense entailing immediate confession, an offense involving suspension, a *saṅghādisesa*.
In this way, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhunīs.
Now at that time, two bhikkhunīs were traveling on the road from Sāketa to Sāvatthī.
Along the way, there was a river to be crossed.
Then those bhikkhunīs approached some boatmen and said to them, “It would be well, friends, if you would ferry us across.”
“Madam, it is not possible for both of us to cross over at once.
So one helped the other across. Once the other had crossed, he violated her.
One who had not crossed over violated one who had not crossed over.
Later, when they gathered together, they asked:
"Noble lady, have you been violated?"
“I have been seduced, noble lady.
But you, noble lady, have not been seduced?
“I too have been seduced, noble lady.”
Then those bhikkhunīs went to Sāvatthī and reported this matter to the bhikkhunīs.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can a bhikkhunī go alone to the other side of a river?"
Then those bhikkhunīs reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] … “Is it true,
bhikkhus, that a bhikkhunī was going alone to the far side of a river?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How indeed, monks, can a bhikkhunī go alone to the other side of a river?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And so, monks, the bhikkhunīs should recite this training rule:

‘If any bhikkhunī should go alone to another village, or should go alone across a river, this bhikkhunī too has committed an offense that is an immediate offense, involving expulsion, a *saṅghādisesa*.’”
Thus was this training rule for the bhikkhunīs laid down by the Blessed One.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhunīs were traveling through the Kosala country toward Sāvatthī and arrived at a certain village in the evening.
There, a certain bhikkhunī was beautiful, pleasing to behold, and inspiring. Upon seeing her, a certain man became infatuated with her.
Then that man, while preparing the beds for those bhikkhunīs, prepared the bed for that bhikkhunī to one side.

Then that bhikkhunī, having observed, “This man is obsessed with lust; if he comes at night, there will be trouble for me,” went to another family without informing the bhikkhunīs and made her bed there.
Then that man, having come in the night, bumped into the bhikkhunīs while searching for her.
Not seeing that bhikkhunī, the bhikkhunīs said, “Without a doubt, that bhikkhunī has gone out with a man.
Then, at the end of that night, the bhikkhunī approached those bhikkhunīs. The bhikkhunīs said this to her: “Noble lady, why did you go out with a man?”
“I did not set out with a man, noble lady.
She reported this matter to the bhikkhunīs.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... [as above]... were indignant, disparaged her, and complained, saying:
“How indeed can a bhikkhunī spend the night alone?
… [as before] … “Is it true, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhunī spends the night alone?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How indeed, monks, can a bhikkhunī spend the night alone?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of the faithful…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, let the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule:
“Whichever bhikkhunī should travel alone to another village, or should cross to the other side of a river alone,
or should stay apart for a night alone— this bhikkhunī too has committed an offense that is an immediate offense, involving expulsion, a *saṅghādisesa*.”
Thus was this training rule for the bhikkhunīs laid down by the Blessed One.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhunīs were traveling along the high road toward Sāvatthī in the Kosala country.
There, a certain bhikkhunī, being pressed by the need to defecate, lagged behind alone and arrived later.
People saw that bhikkhunī and violated her.
Then that bhikkhunī approached those bhikkhunīs. The bhikkhunīs said this to her: “Why have you come alone, noble lady? Are you unharmed?
“I have been harmed, noble ladies.”
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
“How can a bhikkhunī leave the group and stay behind alone? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that a bhikkhunī left the group and stayed behind alone?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How indeed, monks, can a bhikkhunī remain behind, separated from her group?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule as follows:
‘Whichever nun should go alone to another village, or should go alone across a river, or should go alone [to a secluded place]...’”
“If a bhikkhunī should stay away overnight, or if she should remain behind alone after being separated from the group— this bhikkhunī too has committed an offense that is an immediate offense,
involving expulsion, a *saṅghādisesa*. “Whoever,” however, means:
Whichever [nun], of whatever kind …pe… “a nun” …pe… this is the nun intended in this context.
"Or she goes alone to another village":
for one who crosses the enclosure of an enclosed village with her first foot, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
for one who crosses it with her second foot, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
For one who steps across the precincts of an unenclosed village with the first foot, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
For one who steps across with the second foot, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa.
Or, "if she should go to the other side of a river."
In the case of a river, which is defined as that which covers three *maṇḍalas*, if a bhikkhunī crosses anywhere [in such a river] and her inner robe becomes wet:
for one who crosses with the first foot, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*;
for one who crosses with the second foot, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
"Or she should spend one night apart":
when she leaves the reach of the hand of her companion nun at the rising of the dawn, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
Once she has left [the reach], there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
"Or she lags behind from the group":
when she leaves the range of sight or the range of hearing of her companion nun in a forest that is not near a village, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
Once she has left [that range], there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
This too is said with reference to the preceding [offenses].
"An offense of the first entanglement" means:
One incurs [this offense] together with the transgression of the matter itself through failure to admonish.
"Leading to expulsion" means one is expelled from the Saṅgha.
“Saṅghādisesa” ... [as before] ...
for that reason also it is called “saṅghādisesa.
There is no offense:
If the companion nun has departed, or has left the order, or has died, or has gone over to another faction;
or in cases of emergency;
or if she is insane.
"Regarding the first offender":
thus ends the third Saṅghādisesa training rule.
